source.title: Refusal Direction is Universal Across Safety-Aligned Languages
source.authors: Xinpeng Wang; Mingyang Wang; Yihong Liu; Hinrich Schutze; Barbara Plank

record.file_problem: none; the text contains the paper and appendices, with no apparent cut-off or garbling that prevents reading the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies difference-in-means refusal-vector extraction and activation ablation/addition, then evaluates refusal-related behavior in multilingual settings and additional models. This is a direct application of the original intervention in a new setting.
record.gate_note: The main tested results are cross-language harmful-compliance outcomes after ablating or adding refusal vectors. Figure 1 reports the aggregate textual finding across models and safety-aligned target languages; Figure 2 reports aggregate findings by model and source language. Detailed language-by-language chart values are not individually extracted. Table 1 baseline compliance rates are not rows because no refusal-direction intervention is applied. Layer/token sweeps used to select vectors are not rows because they are selection results. The jailbreak-vector experiments in Appendix A.3.3 use a different vector, not the refusal direction, and are not assigned to a claim version.
record.test_reason: The study re-applies the original difference-in-means extraction, all-layer ablation and single-layer addition in a new multilingual setting (14 languages, 10 chat models). It reports harmful-compliance rates, judged by WildGuard, before and after intervention. These are the study's own results on V1 (ablation removes refusal, addition restores it, capability kept) and V6 (a direction from one language transfers to others).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that refusal directions from safety-aligned languages are near-universal. They are approximately parallel across languages, so ablating or adding them modulates refusal cross-lingually. Transfer holds only across safety-aligned languages; Yoruba vectors and targets behave differently. Weak harmful/harmless separation in non-English representations explains cross-lingual jailbreaks.
record.recipe_differences: Uses difference-in-means vectors and residual-stream ablation across layers/positions, as in the original approach, but studies multilingual transfer and evaluates compliance rates with WildGuard rather than relying only on the original refusal-score measure. The paper also uses vector addition and KL filtering when selecting interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Transfer depends on source-language safety alignment: vectors from safety-aligned languages generalize strongly, while Yoruba-derived vectors generalize poorly in some models. The reported effects also vary by target language; Yoruba retains more compliance after addition. Vector selection uses KL filtering and refusal-score ranking, and the selected layer/token positions differ by model and language.

fits_no_version.finding: A 'jailbreak vector' (mean of bypassed minus refused harmful prompts) shifts compliance. Adding it to refused samples gives 20–100% compliance; subtracting it from bypassed samples gives mostly near 0% (Tables 6–7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-lingual jailbreaks move representations along a bypassed-vs-refused direction distinct from the refusal direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Silhouette scores for harmful/harmless separation are higher in English than in other languages (e.g., Llama 0.496 for en vs about 0.22–0.25 for de/th/zh). Authors argue weak harm separation, not the refusal direction, drives multilingual jailbreaks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful/harmless separation at the refusal layer degrades in non-English languages while the refusal direction stays aligned.

record.problems: Most multilingual compliance outcomes are presented as figures without uncertainty estimates in the text. Cross-language prompt data are machine-translated, and non-English outputs are translated back to English for WildGuard evaluation. The capability-retention evidence in Table 8 is for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct only. The paper tests 14 selected languages and acknowledges that results may not extend to extremely low-data languages.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed per-target-language cells from Figures 1–3 and Appendix Figure 9 were not extracted individually; the text-level aggregate findings and explicitly stated examples are retained. The full layer/token sweeps in Figures 10–15 are selection/diagnostic plots. Appendix Tables 6–7 test a different bypass/refusal-derived jailbreak vector rather than the refusal direction in the claim.

untested.parts: Addition was tested only on harmful prompts (it reduced residual compliance). Inducing refusal on harmless prompts was not tested. Capability retention (MMLU, PPL, ARC-C) was reported only for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with the English vector.
Transfer is only across languages within the same model. Transfer between model variants, or from base to instruct models, was not tested.

missing.what: Ablation with vectors derived from Yoruba: poor transfer for Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B, relatively better for gemma-2-9b-it.
Ablation with vectors derived from ja, ko and ru: strong transfer across most target languages for all three models.

record.verdict_notes: Most per-language results are figure-only, with no uncertainty reported. Compliance is judged by WildGuard on machine back-translations. Vector selection uses KL filtering (at most 0.2). Appendix B notes occasional 'shallow jailbreaks' (complying but writing benign content) after ablation. The record's 'random vector' controls are other candidate diff-in-means vectors. T3 rather than T1 because the setting is new and the main measure is WildGuard compliance rather than the original's refusal/safety scores.

versions.untested_parts: Tests harmful-request compliance after refusal-direction ablation and reports capability measures for one model. It does not test whether adding the direction induces refusals to harmless requests, or establish capability preservation across all models and abilities.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration procedure is evaluated.
No external jailbreak is tested for suppression of the refusal direction, and no training against its ablation is performed.
Cross-language vector similarity is examined, but the study does not compare a single direction with affine, cone, or multi-direction accounts.
The paper discusses separate harmfulness and refusal processes by reference to prior work, but does not test that distinction with its own results.
Tests within-model transfer across languages. It does not transfer a vector between different model variants, or test transfer from base to instruct models.
The study compares source languages with different safety-alignment quality, but does not vary how or when refusal training is done.

relationships.condition: Ablation of the selected direction (English, zh, de or th source) on harmful prompts in safety-aligned languages, across 10 chat models; Llama-3.1-8B capability check.
relationships.reason: Compliance rises substantially for all models (E1–E10) and nears or exceeds 90% (Z1–T3). Refusal falls from 0.99 to 0.02 with MMLU, PPL and ARC-C nearly unchanged (C1–C4). Other candidate vectors fail (R1, R5). Addition drives compliance near 0% (A1–A9).
relationships.display_finding: Ablation increased compliance across all 10 models, reaching approximately 90% or higher in tested language settings; Llama-3.1-8B refusal fell from 0.99 to 0.02 with MMLU, perplexity, and ARC-C nearly unchanged, other candidate vectors failed, and addition drove compliance near 0%.

relationships.condition: Vectors sourced from safety-aligned languages (en, zh, de, th) applied to other languages in the same model.
relationships.reason: Cross-language ablation collapses refusal (E1–E10, Z1–T3). Ablation also raises Yoruba compliance (EY1, ZY1–ZY3). Cross-language addition restores refusal (A1–A9). Directions are highly aligned across languages (G1–G3).

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: Ablation of the selected direction (English, zh, de or th source) on harmful prompts in safety-aligned languages, across 10 chat models; Llama-3.1-8B capability check.
labels.reason: Table 8: refusal rate 0.99->0.02, with MMLU 68.5->68.0, PPL 8.65->8.71 and ARC-C 52.4->52.5. The text reports a substantial compliance increase for all 10 models. Minor: zh/de/th ablation and addition used only 3 models, and A2-A9 are not all linked to V1.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.condition: Addition evaluated on Yoruba, a safety-misaligned language.
labels.reason: §5.4: Yoruba falls only 58%->28% (gemma-2-9b-it) and keeps higher residual compliance for all three source vectors. The direction is English-derived, so this overlaps with the V6 limit; there was no same-language Yoruba addition.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: Vectors sourced from safety-aligned languages (en, zh, de, th) applied to other languages in the same model.
labels.reason: §5.2-5.3: cross-language ablation gives near-total refusal collapse (about 90%+ compliance). Addition reduces compliance; heatmaps over en/zh/de/th show aligned directions. §A.4: ja/ko/ru vectors also transfer.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.condition: Yoruba as target of added vectors, or as source language of the vector.
labels.reason: AY1 is partial (58%->28%). §A.4 says Yoruba-derived vectors generalize poorly in Llama/Qwen and better in Gemma (figure only). That is partial, not absent, so limits_scope rather than challenges.

relation.reason: It runs causal ablation and addition and reports compliance rates before and after (Figures 1-3, Table 8).

tranche.reason: Same difference-in-means extraction, all-layer ablation and single-layer addition as the original. The measure differs (WildGuard compliance after back-translation), and the setting is new (14 languages). The study has its own results on the claim.

source_check.notes: Table 1 gives numeric baselines for Llama3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B and gemma2-9B, so the E5/E7/E10/Z/D/T/A rows need not be figure-only. The paper's numbers disagree in places: gemma Yoruba baseline 0.57 / 58% / 56.6%, Qwen Yoruba 74.9 (prose) vs 74.0 (table), and Qwen peak layers 15–29 vs 15-19. WildGuard counts benign 'shallow jailbreak' replies as compliance.

statements.correction: zh/de/th-vector ablation was run only on gemma-2-9B-it, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (§5.3). EY1's target is Yoruba, which the study treats as safety-misaligned (Table 1 gemma2-9B yo baseline 56.6%). zh/de/th ablation also raises gemma-2-9B-it Yoruba compliance from about 58% to over 90%.
statements.problem: The conditions say targets are safety-aligned or higher-resource, but EY1's target is Yoruba, which the study calls safety-misaligned. The text also reads as if the zh/de/th tests covered all 10 models.

statements.correction: If it cites this study: Yoruba-derived vectors show 'poor generalization' across most languages (figure only, Fig 9d, §A.4). This is clearest in Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, and better in gemma-2-9B. That is a partial transfer failure, not an absent effect stated with numbers.
statements.problem: The statement is cut off. The visible text makes no claim about this study and cites no rows from it.

statements.correction: gemma-2-9b-it, English vector added at one layer: Yoruba compliance 58%->28%; most other languages reach 0% (§5.4). Yoruba keeps higher residual compliance for en, de and th vectors, varying by model. Ablation does transfer into Yoruba: en vector 0.57->0.87; zh/de/th vectors about 58% to over 90% (gemma-2-9B-it).
statements.problem: 58%->28% is right, but it is a partial reduction, and the record labels it V6 limits_scope. It does not meet the challenges bar (effect absent or reversed).
Minor: the authors name safety alignment, not resource level, as the condition. They call Thai and Polish mid/low-resource, and Thai vectors transfer.

statements.correction: en/de/th vectors are added at one layer of the unmodified model (§5.4). This lowers baseline harmful compliance, with most languages reaching about 0%. Gemma-2-9b-it Yoruba falls only 58%->28%. Tested on Llama-3.1-8B, gemma-2-9b-it and Qwen2.5-7B only.
statements.problem: 'Cross-language addition restores refusal' misreads the experiment: addition was applied to the unablated model, not after ablation.
